scouting.text: Inspect the undersides of lower-canopy leaves first; look for yellow-orange powder below yellow spots.
Photograph the whole plant and both the upper and lower surface of suspect leaves.
Check leaf edges and tips where water collects; spots often start there.
Walk the marked priority points, starting with the highest rank, and record what you find at each.
Priority point 1: the reported plant and its immediate neighbours.
Priority point 2: about 45 m south-west of the reported plant.
Priority point 3: about 40 m south of the reported plant.
Priority point 4: about 40 m east of the reported plant.
Priority point 5: about 40 m north of the reported plant.

recommendations.text: Mark the affected area and avoid moving leaves, plant material, soil or tools out of it.
After visiting affected trees, wash clothing and clean footwear and tools before entering other plots.
Plan to re-inspect in 4-6 weeks: lesions from recent infections appear after this delay.
Count rust spots on a sample of leaves. Rwandan extension guidance considers control when there are about two spots per leaf; discuss with your extension officer before acting.
Keep recommended tree spacing and prune to open the bush. In a Rwandan farm survey, pruning, mulching and fertilising were linked with less rust, and intercropping with more.
Before any fungicide use, consult your local extension officer; follow the product label exactly.
Remove unmanaged (feral) coffee plants and competing weeds near the plot.
For future planting, ask about rust-resistant coffee varieties suited to your area.

reasons.text: Evidence is not specific; an expert should confirm before decisions.
Another condition with similar signs may be present; an expert can tell them apart.

condition.label: Possible coffee leaf rust
condition.confidence_kind: uncalibrated evidence score from image signals; not a probability of infection
condition.uncertainty: Image signals are consistent with coffee leaf rust (evidence score 0.77). This is not a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis. Signals of another problem (Cercospora leaf spot (brown eye spot)) are also present; a reviewer should distinguish them.

severity.scale: OIRSA leaf-area classes as used by RoCoLe
severity.scope: Leaf-level severity of the photographed leaf, not plot incidence.

weather_risk.summary: Recent or forecast weather was sometimes favourable for rust infection.
weather_risk.method: Hourly infection-favourability heuristic: wet hour (RH >= wet_rh_pct or precipitation >= wet_precip_mm) weighted by a trapezoidal temperature factor; a day is favourable when it contains a wet spell >= min_wet_hours with mean temperature factor >= min_temp_factor.
weather_risk.interpretation: Infection-favourable weather suitability class; not a probability of infection or disease.

temperature_c.note: Germination bounds/optimum from review citing De Jong et al. 1987; linear ramps between bounds are an assumption.

min_wet_hours.note: Lower end of the 6-24 h wetness reported for germination.

wet_rh_pct.note: Assumption: RH >= 90% used as a leaf-wetness proxy; no leaf-wetness sensor data. Uncalibrated.

wet_precip_mm.note: Free water from rain is required for germination; threshold is an assumption.

classes.note: Class thresholds on fraction of favourable days are uncalibrated assumptions.

latent_period_days.note: Characteristic lesions appear 4-6 weeks after infection.

cross_source_check.note: Small sample; ERA5 lags ~5 days so only early overlap days exist. Not a bias correction.

climatology.technical_note: Baseline is ERA5 reanalysis; the current window is operational model/forecast data. Their wetness differs (see cross_source_check); treat the relation as indicative only.
climatology.summary: This is more often favourable than usual for these dates here (2015-2024 reanalysis).
climatology.caveat: The long-term baseline uses a different weather dataset than the current period, so this comparison is only indicative.

limitations: Leaf wetness approximated from relative humidity/precipitation of gridded model data; canopy conditions differ.

Saturates in persistently humid zones (>0.9 favourable days in ERA5 for Chinchiná, Colombia, in both epidemic and non-epidemic years): 'high' means weather is not limiting, not that an epidemic is likely.
Ignores inoculum, host susceptibility, shade, fruit load and management.
weather_risk.validation: Consistency check only (docs/backend/model.md); not validated against incidence data.

map.limitations: Relative scouting priority (0-1) around reported points; not an infection probability. Uncalibrated distance decay and wind stretch.
map.method: Relative scouting priority on a local grid: exponential distance decay from reported symptomatic points, stretched downwind when forecast wind direction is consistent; reduced near prior observations reported clear. Weather favourability is reported separately (farm-level). Not an infection probability.

guidance_scope.applicability: Biology (free water, temperature range, latency, dispersal, lower-canopy onset) is pathogen-level and applies across regions. Practical guidance is drawn mainly from Hawaiʻi extension publications; only generic measures (inspection, sanitation, movement limits, re-scouting, consulting extension, resistant cultivars) are retained. Hawaiʻi-specific regulatory reporting, product lists and contacts are deliberately omitted. Rwanda-specific guidance (RAB/Plantwise 2012) and a Rwandan farm survey (Bigirimana et al. 2012) were added; product names and doses in the RAB factsheet are intentionally not reproduced.

regional_context.text: Rwanda: a 2012 survey of 307 farms found rust in all provinces (worst in Eastern Province), less rust at higher altitude, and all commercial varieties susceptible.
